name: Flutter Kicks
tierNote: Safety tier C (content.md 5.1: not in the A or B lists); census.json difficulty tier 2.

claims.text: Lie on the floor, legs straight, arms by the sides, palms flat on the floor.

quotes.text: Lie on the floor with your legs straight, arms to your sides, and palms flat against the ground.
quotes.where: How to do Flutter Kicks, step 1

claims.text: With the lower back touching the floor, lift the feet several inches off the floor.

quotes.text: With your lower back in contact with the floor, take a breath and lift your feet several inches off the floor.
quotes.where: How to do Flutter Kicks, step 2

claims.text: Move the legs up and down alternately in short, crisp movements.

quotes.text: Take another breath and begin moving your legs up and down alternatingly. Keep your movements short and crisp.
quotes.where: How to do Flutter Kicks, step 3

claims.text: Squeeze the shoulder blades down and together and use the abs to flatten the lower back to the floor; it needs to stay that way throughout.

quotes.text: Lying on your back, squeeze your shoulder blades down and together and use your abdominals to flatten your lower back to the floor. This needs to remain the same throughout

claims.text: Both feet come off the floor with the knees straight, and the legs kick from the hips.

quotes.text: Next raise both feet off the floor with straight knees and essentially kick your legs at the hips

claims.text: Keeping the lower back flat on the floor at all times keeps the abs working and doing most of the work of holding the legs up.

quotes.text: An important tip for a safe and effective flutter kick is to keep your lower back flat against the floor at all times. Doing so ensures that your abs stay engaged, provide stability, and do most of the work involved in keeping your legs in the air and moving.

claims.text: A common mistake is arching the lower back, which stresses the spine and makes the abs work less; keep the lower back on the floor from start to finish.

quotes.text: A common mistake with the movement and numerous other ab exercises is arching the lower back. Doing so places unnecessary stress on your spine and lengthens the abs, preventing them from engaging as effectively.
quotes.where: Mistakes to Avoid, Arching Your Lower Back

quotes.text: Avoid the error by keeping your lower back in contact with the floor from start to finish.
quotes.where: Mistakes to Avoid, Arching Your Lower Back

claims.text: Short, controlled leg motions keep balance and the spine in a healthy position; uncontrolled legs make the lower back more likely to arch.

quotes.text: The second tip for kicks is keeping the leg motions short and controlled. Doing so is vital for maintaining your balance and keeping your spine in a healthy position. Moving your legs uncontrollably leads to instability and increases the risk of arching your lower back.

claims.text: The second mistake is moving the legs through a large range; the kicks should be short and quick.

quotes.text: The second mistake with flutter kicks is moving your legs through an extended range of motion. Doing so isn’t necessarily fatal, but the objective is to perform short and quick leg motions, alternating numerous times per set.
quotes.where: Mistakes to Avoid, Moving Your Legs Too Much

claims.text: The exercise works the hip flexors and the core: the rectus abdominis holds the legs up and the hip flexors help hold and move them.

quotes.text: The primary muscle that works during the exercise is the rectus abdominis.
Kicks also engage the five hip flexors. The collection of muscles assists the abs in keeping our legs in the air and moving up and down.
This exercise works your hip flexors and core

claims.text: It should be pain free, or not raise existing pain, during the exercise, after it and the next day; some delayed muscle soreness 48-72 hours later is normal if it stays manageable.

quotes.text: Like any exercise this should be pain free or shouldn’t increase existing pain levels, during, after and the next day.
It is normal to feel some delayed onset muscle soreness between 48-72 hours but this should be manageable

claims.text: For endurance: 30-50 kicks to fatigue, 3-5 sets, rests of 30 seconds at most; to make it harder, add ankle weights progressively.

quotes.text: For endurance you should perform 30-50 kicks to fatigue
You should perform 3-5 sets with no more than 30 second rests
To make this exercise harder you can add ankles weight progressively

claims.text: Breathe as steadily as you can.

quotes.text: Breathe as steadily as you can and go for as long as your abs allow you.
quotes.where: How to do Flutter Kicks, step 4

claims.text: One coach says the way many people do flutter kicks, legs held a few inches up while kicking, creates a big arch in the lower back and is a recipe for lower back pain.

quotes.text: The way that many people perform flutter kicks is a recipe for lower back pain.

As explained in the video above, they’ll lie on their back, hold their legs up a few inches from the ground and begin to flutter away. However, from the example shown, this creates a big arch in the lower back.

claims.text: A lower-ab workout that includes flutter kicks gives the safety tip to stop if it hurts.

quotes.text: When performing any workout program, there are always safety tips to remember. Lower ab exercises are no different.
Stop if it hurts.

plate.viewWhy: The lower back flat on the floor (c4, c6) and its fault, the arch (c7), and the small vertical kick (c3, c9) are sagittal.
plate.frames: Cycle convention: one half-cycle, one leg a few inches higher and the other lower, then switched; Trace follows the near foot. The two poses barely differ (census note).
plate.start: Lying on the back, arms by the sides, palms flat (c1); shoulder blades down, lower back flat on the floor (c4); both legs straight with the feet several inches off the floor (c2, c5).
plate.end: Near leg a little higher, far leg a little lower, knees straight, short range (c3, c5, c9); lower back still flat (c4).

checkpoints.what: Abs flatten the lower back to the floor, and it stays there.

checkpoints.label: Feet lifted
checkpoints.what: Both feet several inches off the floor, knees straight.

checkpoints.label: Short kicks

mistake.what: Lower back arches up off the floor as the legs kick.
mistake.why: LR-31 step 1: Fitness Volt says many people do flutter kicks in a way that creates a big arch in the lower back, a recipe for lower back pain (c14); Hevy says arching puts unnecessary stress on the spine (c7), and bigger, uncontrolled kicks make it more likely (c8).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: the lower back arching off the floor (c14, c7). Fitness Volt's "The way that many people perform flutter kicks is a recipe for lower back pain." is followed by "As explained in the video above, they’ll lie on their back, hold their legs up a few inches from the ground and begin to flutter away. However, from the example shown, this creates a big arch in the lower back." (c14, 'Crucial form tips'): many people make this fault of this exercise, the arch, named in the next sentence; it is one fault, not a list (D-SUP-LB7-DIPREPS reading). No other fault passes step 1. Set aside: Hevy's "A common mistake with the movement and numerous other ab exercises is arching the lower back." (c7) opens the first item of its 'Mistakes to Avoid' list, a list sentence, and is not counted (R-LB4-2); counted, it picks the same fault. Fitness Volt's "As far as reps go, the flutter kick is commonly performed in a four-count fashion." ('Sets/reps') is a counting format, not a fault; its "some people might place their hands or fists under their butt or lower back to prevent the arching" has no frequency word and is an aid. Hevy's "do most of the work" (c6) is about the abs' work and "Unlike many ab movements" is about the cable crunch, another exercise; Healthline's "Many different exercises engage the lower abdominal muscles." is about exercises. Step 2 is not needed; the same fault is also the one most tied to harm: Hevy "Doing so places unnecessary stress on your spine" (c7); Fitness Volt "a recipe for lower back pain" (c14) and "The psoas muscle, which is one of the hip flexors, pulls on the spine, therefore, causing some real discomfort." Harm quotes set aside: Hevy's "increases the risk of arching your lower back" (c8) ties uncontrolled kicks to the arch, not to harm; Hevy's 'Moving Your Legs Too Much' says "Doing so isn’t necessarily fatal" (c9), which states no harm; Fitness Volt's "otherwise it’s useless and dangerous" names no fault, and its bent-leg "could also further reduce the strain on your lower back" is a variation; Hawkes' "this should be pain free" (c11) and Healthline's "Stop if it hurts." (c15) name no fault; Fitness Volt's "It protects your lower back from straining whether lifting weights, doing basic activities, or just walking for long hours at a time." and "you’ll be less prone to injuries" and Healthline's "A strong core can help improve posture, prevent injuries, and relieve back pain." are benefits; Fitness Volt's "due to the stress being placed on the core muscles" is training stress, not harm. Step 3 gives the same fault: Hevy's 'Mistakes to Avoid' list, written for this exercise, runs 1 'Arching Your Lower Back' (c7), 2 'Moving Your Legs Too Much' (c9); Fitness Volt's 'Crucial form tips' names only the arch; Hawkes and Healthline have no mistakes list. drawable stays true: the side view shows the lower back lifted off the floor, a still sign. Pick unchanged; handlingMistakes[0] is already the arch.

tells.text: Lower back stays on the floor

tempo.text: Cycle: short, crisp alternating kicks (c3); sets of 30-50 kicks for endurance (c12). Up, down and pause stay null (LR-33, R-LB7-6). Decided against 2 s / 1 s: no quote on the card asks for a slow lowering, and the read sources disagree on speed. Hevy says "Keep your movements short and crisp." (c3) and "short and quick leg motions" (c9); Healthline's flutter steps say "Slowly lower your right leg a few inches while simultaneously lifting your left leg a few inches." (not cited on the card); Fitness Volt says "you can vary the tempo based on your goals" with a slower pace for the abs (not cited). The kick is an alternating cycle in which one leg lowers while the other lifts, so there is no single lowering phase to slow, and the WEAK convention would side with one source against the anchor. No quote asks for a pause, hold or squeeze in the kick. Fitness Volt's interval option, 30 s of kicks and 10-15 s rest, is a set format, not a phase time.

grip.note: Hand archetype none: palms rest flat on the floor by the sides (c1).

setup.step: Lie on your back, legs straight, arms at your sides, palms flat.
Squeeze your shoulder blades down and flatten your lower back.
Lift both feet several inches, knees straight.
Kick your legs up and down, alternating, in short quick moves.

posture.point: Lower back flat on the floor.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Lower back arches off the floor.
handlingMistakes.fix: Use your abs to flatten it again.
Keep the kicks short and controlled.

rows.means: Your abs hold your legs up.
Your hip flexors move and hold the legs.

rows.where: Pain in the lower back, during, after or the next day
rows.means: This exercise should not cause or raise pain.
rows.fix: Stop the set. Don't train through the pain.

risks.risk: An arched lower back puts stress on the spine.
Uncontrolled kicks make the back more likely to arch.

zooms.right: Lower back pressed flat to the floor.
zooms.wrong: Lower back arched off the floor.

libraryDiff.why: Library: hip_flexors primary; abs secondary. Hevy ranks the rectus abdominis as the primary muscle, with the hip flexors assisting (c10), and says the abs do most of the work of holding the legs up (c6). Hawkes names the hip flexors and core without ranking them (c10). Proposed: abs primary, hip_flexors secondary (ruling R-W0-4). A proposal for the LIB data card.
